item.title: Optimizing Sepsis Time Zero Definitions Through Associations between Antibiotic Timing and Mortality
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Sepsis performance measures require operational definitions of "time zero", but SEP-1's heterogeneous organ dysfunction criteria may not all identify patients vulnerable to harm from antibiotic delays.

Objectives: To determine which SEP-1 organ dysfunctions identify patients in whom antibiotic delays are associated with increased mortality.

Methods: We analyzed adults with suspected infection using electronic health record data from 145 U.S. hospitals (2018-2023). We estimated associations between antibiotic timing (1-3 vs. 0-1h and 3-6 vs. 0-3h) and in-hospital mortality for each SEP-1 organ dysfunction criterion, alone and in combination: hypotension, elevated lactate, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy. We used inverse probability weighting to adjust for baseline and time-varying confounders.

Measurements and main results: Among 1,849,729 encounters with suspected infection, 624,416 had ≥1 organ dysfunction and received antibiotics within 6h of time zero. Antibiotics at 1-3 vs. 0-1h were associated with higher mortality when time zero was defined by hypotension (aRR 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.10) or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L (aRR 1.10; 1.05-1.15), but not for other dysfunctions alone or in combination. Among patients without hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, antibiotics at 3-6 vs. 0-3h were only associated with higher mortality in patients with acute respiratory failure (aRR 1.11; 1.05-1.18).

Conclusions: Mortality associations with antibiotics beyond 1 hour were most evident when sepsis time zero was defined by hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, and with antibiotics beyond 3 hours when defined by acute respiratory failure. These findings could inform refinements to sepsis time zero definitions to better guide antibiotic urgency and performance measurement.

item.title: Systemic Inflammation in Bronchiectasis: Data from the EMBARC-BRIDGE Study
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Background: Neutrophilic inflammation in the airways is associated with exacerbation risk in patients with bronchiectasis. Systemic inflammation and neutrophil function are less characterised. The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between systemic inflammation and neutrophil function with severity of disease and clinical outcomes.

Methods: Observational international multi-centre study of adults with bronchiectasis (EMBARC-BRIDGE). Serum inflammatory profiling was performed in 487 patients using Olink® proteomics, and associations with key clinical and patient reported outcomes, including severe exacerbations during follow-up, were analysed. In a sub-study, peripheral blood neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients and controls were analysed for surface activation and functional markers, and functional responses including degranulation and neutrophil extracellular trap formation.

Results: Systemic inflammatory profiling revealed a dominant neutrophil-endothelial signature. Several proteins including PR3, AZU1, MPO, the soluble IL-33 receptor ST2, and the cellular stress marker GDF-15 were associated with increased disease severity using the bronchiectasis severity index, lower lung function, increased symptoms and for many markers, higher rates of severe exacerbations during follow-up. Neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients exhibited reduced surface CD11b and increased CXCR2, with lower CD11b correlating with lower lung function. Basal degranulation was reduced in bronchiectasis, whereas responsiveness to LPS stimulation was preserved.

Conclusion: Bronchiectasis is associated with a systemic neutrophil and endothelial inflammatory signature linked to disease severity and risk of severe exacerbations, alongside altered but functionally-responsive circulating neutrophils.

Hughes C, Long MB, Stobo J, Johnson ED, Viligorska K, Lind H
